idiom_name: trait AsAny { fn as_any(&self) -> &dyn Any } + downcast_ref<T>()
implementation_notes: The idiomatic Rust answer is static - an extension trait, a trait with default methods or an enum of alternatives keeps the base trait closed and the compiler seeing every capability - so runtime negotiation is the escape hatch, and this is its portable form: the queryable trait makes Any a supertrait and every implementor (or a blanket impl) forwards self as &dyn Any, after which clients call thing.as_any().downcast_ref::<Concrete>() and read None as 'unsupported'. The boilerplate exists because a &dyn Trait does not coerce to &dyn Any before trait upcasting (see the sibling variant), and calling downcast_ref directly on the trait object would test the trait object's own type, not the concrete type behind it.
pitfalls: Any requires 'static, so an extension interface cannot be implemented for a type that borrows - negotiated capabilities cannot carry lifetimes.
A blanket as_any() impl requires the method to stay object-safe (where Self: Sized) or dyn Component becomes impossible.
Every adapter or decorator must forward as_any(), otherwise wrapping silently erases the capability.

variants.name: Trait upcasting to &dyn Any (Rust 1.86+)
variants.implementation_notes: Since Rust 1.86 a trait object can be upcast to its supertrait, so declaring trait Component: Any makes (c as &dyn Any).downcast_ref::<TextAccessor>() legal without any as_any() boilerplate; the cast stays explicit at the query site, and the 'static and exact-concrete-type limits of Any still apply. Choose this variant when the toolchain is 1.86 or newer and the queryable trait can declare Any as a supertrait.
pitfalls: Trait upcasting needs the supertrait bound to be object-safe and 'static; older MSRVs must fall back to as_any().
Forgetting the explicit cast makes downcast_ref test the trait object's own type and always fail, usually looking like 'the extension is never supported'.
